slides.title: Can this really work?
slides.text: Rules are promises. This story shows the cryptography that keeps them: which keys exist, what each step does to them, and the few things no cryptography can do.
slides.deep: Two mechanisms carry everything: encryption for read (keys you hold or don't) and signature verification for every other operation (checked by each peer on every change). The limits are listed honestly at the end.

slides.title: Four kinds of keys.
slides.text: Each one has exactly one job.
list: Seal: signs a piece of data's first rule, then is destroyed.
Identity key: your lock. Each of your devices also publishes a lock of its own, grown from its passkey.
Role key: a lock all members of a role can open.
Data key: the key the data itself is encrypted with.
slides.deep: Ed25519 for signing (seal, signers). X25519, later hybrid X-Wing with ML-KEM, for locks. Data keys are 256-bit symmetric keys used with an AEAD (XChaCha20-Poly1305). Wrapping follows HPKE (RFC 9180).

slides.title: Data is born.
slides.text: Your device makes a fresh seal. Its public half becomes the data's ID. It signs the first rule, naming the owner, and the private half is wiped. From now on, only the owner can change the rules.
slides.deep: The genesis certificate: data ID = seal public key, first rule = {owner, everything}, signature by the seal. Then the secret is zeroised. Any later rule must chain back to this certificate.

slides.title: Reading is a chain of envelopes.
slides.text: The content is encrypted with the data key. The data key sits in an {envelope} for the owner and for every role that may read. The role key sits in an envelope for every member. Your identity key opens the first envelope, and the chain opens the rest.
slides.deep: Three envelopes: identity key → role key → data key → content. Each envelope is an HPKE seal of one key to another key's public half. The keyring travels with the data, so no server ever holds keys.

slides.title: Writing is a chain of signatures.
slides.text: Mia ticks “buy milk”. Her signer signs the change. Every device that receives it checks three links before merging: the signer acts for Mia, Mia is in “home”, and “home” has update on this list. One broken link, and the change is dropped.
slides.deep: Every peer checks a change before merging: the signature, the signer's registration in the identity's history, the identity's role membership, and a rule covering this operation on this data. Any broken link: dropped.

slides.title: Adding Mia to a role: one envelope.
slides.text: The owner puts the role key in an envelope for Mia's identity key. That's all. Mia can now read everything the role can read, including what came before she joined.
slides.deep: One HPKE envelope of the current role key to Mia's identity key, signed by the owner. Older role keys are reachable through back-links, so Mia reads the history too.

slides.title: Giving a rule: read needs a key, everything else needs only a signature.
slides.text: Giving “plumber” read on the tap item puts the item's data key in an envelope for the plumber role. Giving update needs no key at all: it's a signed rule change in the item's history, and every device enforces it.
slides.deep: Read needs the data key wrapped for the role key. Every other operation needs only a signed rule. That rule sits in the data's rule set, a grow-only set of signed certificates merged by union.

slides.title: Removing someone means new keys.
slides.text: The plumber still knows the old role key. So the role gets a new one, in envelopes for the remaining members only. Every piece of data the role reads gets a new data key the next time it changes. This is {rotation}: the plumber loses the future, and his honest devices forget the past.
flow: new data key on next change
slides.deep: The role key rotates and is wrapped for the remaining members. Each piece of data the role reads gets a new data key on its next write (lazy rotation), because the old one is known to the removed member.

slides.title: Taking a rule away.
slides.text: Taking update away is just a signed rule change. Taking read away rotates the data key, and the new one goes to the owner and every reading role except that one.
slides.deep: Taking read from a role rotates that data key immediately; the new key is wrapped for the owner and the remaining reading roles. Taking any other operation is only a signed rule change; no key turns.

slides.title: Losing your phone.
slides.text: Your identity named its next signer when it was born, so you can switch to it. Then your identity key turns, and every role you're in gets a new role key, so the lost phone opens nothing new.
flow: new key for every role you're in
slides.deep: Pre-rotation: the identity's birth record committed to the hash of its next signer key. A stolen device also held role keys, so every role the identity is in rotates, as if the identity had been removed.

slides.title: Two things at once.
slides.text: Mia edits the list on a train, offline, at the same moment you remove her. When both devices meet, the removal wins: her edit is dropped everywhere. Every device decides the same way, so they all end up agreeing.
slides.deep: Concurrency is resolved toward less authority: a removal and a change made without seeing it count as concurrent, and the removal wins. Every peer applies the same deterministic rule, so all copies converge.

slides.title: Heal the future, forget the past.
slides.text: A CRDT needs its history, so old keys can't simply be deleted, and full {forward secrecy} for live history is impossible. Three layers get close. Keys turn regularly, so a stolen key soon opens nothing new. At stable points, the past is cut, resealed, and the old keys are deleted for good. And older keys a device rarely needs sit behind a fresh tap of your passkey, out of reach of a thief or of malware.
list: Forget: cut at stable points, delete the old keys.
Lock away: older keys only open with a fresh tap.
slides.deep: Heal: post-compromise security through regular rotation (decided). Forget: true forward secrecy before a stable cut (D35, open). Lock away: archive keys sealed under a PRF-derived key, released only after user verification (D37, proposed).

slides.title: What no cryptography can do, and why that's fine.
slides.text: Whatever someone once saw, they can remember, screenshot or copy. That's true of every app today, and no system can change it. What we can promise is the rest.
list: Nothing new: rotation keeps the future out.
Nothing kept, on honest devices: the next step.
Read is per piece of data, so what you share alone is its own data.
slides.deep: The analogue hole is real for every system: whatever a reader saw can be copied. Read granularity equals key granularity, so a part shared on its own must be its own data.

slides.title: Ended means forgotten.
slides.text: The moment a device meets any peer that holds an ending, a revoke or a lapse, it applies it like a {delete trigger}: it wipes the keys and the plaintext copies of everything it may no longer read. It happens offline-first and without a server, on every honest device, the plumber's included.

then: keep only sealed bytes, if a carrier

slides.deep: An ending (revoke or lapse) is a signed event in the history. On learning it, an honest device deletes the affected data keys and decrypted copies. A carrier keeps only sealed bytes, which it could never open.

slides.title: Envelopes only for keys you can trust.
slides.text: Each device publishes its lock, an encryption key, in its identity's history, signed by its own signer. Envelopes may only be made for locks found there, and only by someone a rule allows. Otherwise an attacker could slip in a lock of their own, and writers would quietly encrypt to them.
slides.action: Where does the data key live?
slides.deep: Each device's lock is published in its identity's history, signed by its registered signer. Envelopes go only to locks found there, so nobody can inject a key of their own (Keyhive's open gap G2).

slides.title: Where does the data key live?
slides.text: Nobody holds it for the data. It travels with the data itself: every piece of data carries a small {keyring} next to its rules. The keyring holds the data key in envelopes: one for the owner, one for each role that may read. Carriers store it like everything else, sealed and unreadable.
slides.deep: The keyring: current epoch, one envelope per reader (owner and reading roles), and back-links where each data key decrypts the previous one, like Keyhive's causal encryption. Forward secrecy is given up for live history, on purpose.

slides.title: Which key turns when.
slides.text: Only read changes keys. A new data key always opens the one before it, so whoever may read now can still read the history.

head: Step
Identity key
Role key
Data key
rows: Two of the owner's devices rotate at once
both kept, until the next rotation

slides.deep: Only read touches keys. Concurrent rotations of the same key are both kept until the next rotation, BeeKEM's approach to concurrent updates. Large roles may manage their role key with BeeKEM later (D20, proposed).

slides.title: The whole machine.
list: Data is born with a seal that is used once and destroyed.
Read is a chain of envelopes: identity key, role key, data key.
Everything else is a chain of signatures, checked by every device.
Removing someone rotates keys: they lose the future, and honest devices forget the past.
slides.deep: Seal → owner → rules for roles. Read: identity key → role key → data key. Everything else: signature chains checked by every peer. Endings win, rotate keys and wipe copies.
